findings.reason: The protected Python solution groups shifted strings by computing a canonical signature for each string based on the modular difference (mod 26) between consecutive characters. Strings with the same signature belong to the same shifting sequence and are grouped into a hash table. The solution runs in O(L) time and O(L) space where L is the total number of characters across all strings; no candidate is required.

Shift-equivalence requires all adjacent character differences to be congruent modulo 26. Mapping each string to a tuple of (ord(string[i]) - ord(string[i-1])) % 26 creates a unique, shift-invariant key for every equivalence class.

Computing the tuple key for a string of length k takes O(k) time. Processing all strings with total character count L takes O(L) time and O(L) space to store the grouped strings. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts list of strings, returning a list of lists of strings grouped by shifting sequence.

The approach accurately details shift-invariant tuple encoding, hash map grouping, and O(L) time/space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover 'a'-normalization strategies, single-character empty-tuple keys, and circular alphabet wraparound.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical modular-difference tuple key hashing algorithm with SHA-256 digests 63801079169a39b794e7d065515ca41eacebbd89e5829fca3d1c139d62cd6fed and 0e3d106b9df67d361a4c4212b1ace2e6b6a11b246a53ef54c792365e11141d7c.
